real_s1.explanation: Across these dog and other furry-animal classes, the unit is clearly least active when the main subject faces right. It is more active for subjects facing left, and also when the subject faces toward or away from the camera. This right-facing aversion is the most distinctive property of the unit. It held strongly on new photos, for left vs right and for left vs no clear direction, while similar units only partly share it. The unit also prefers large, frame-filling, sharp subjects, but similar units share most of that preference. The apparent preference for subjects cut off by the frame edge did not hold on new photos.

real_s2.explanation: This dog-class unit is most distinctive in being weak when the main subject faces or points to the right. It responds more when the subject faces left, faces toward or away from the camera, or has no clear facing direction. The left-over-right difference is at the top of its layer and replicated strongly on new photos (d +1.34). Left over no-clear-facing also replicated. The other preferences are weaker or shared with similar units, which also reach the 95th percentile on those rows. These include large, cropped subjects filling the frame, frames without visible straight lines, and facing the camera over facing right. The preference for subjects cut off by the frame edge did not replicate.

real_s3.explanation: Among its top dog classes, this unit responds most to dogs and similar furry animals seen frontally or facing left, filling much of the frame. What is particular to it is a left-right asymmetry: it is clearly weaker when the subject faces right than when it faces left, and left-facing subjects also beat photos with no clear facing direction or no single subject. Both of these held on new photos. The strong preference for frontal over right-facing views (row 4) is shared with its similar units. The preferences for large subjects, subjects cut off by the border and no visible straight lines are either shared with similar units or did not hold up on new photos.

null_s1.explanation: The clearest signal is a preference, shared with similar units, for dogs that face toward or away from the camera and fill a large part of the frame. Subjects in profile, small subjects and scenes with no single main subject drive the unit less. The features that looked particular to this unit did not replicate on new photos: the left-over-right facing asymmetry (Rows 1 and 3) and the preference for subjects cut off by the frame edge (Row 10) both fell to about the 50th percentile. So nothing in the table reliably separates this unit from its neighbours. What is left is a general response to close, frame-filling, frontal subjects.

null_s2.explanation: This unit responds to dogs across many breeds. The left-versus-right facing preference, the preference for subjects cut off by the frame edge, and the left-versus-no-clear-direction difference all vanished on new photos, so they look like noise from small samples. The strongest remaining signal is a stronger response when the dog faces toward or away from the camera than when it faces right. A weaker signal is a stronger response for large, prominent subjects than for small ones. Its similar units share both of these, so they are not particular to this unit. I can't confidently name anything distinctive about it.

null_s3.explanation: The unit's strongest effects are ones it shares with its most similar units. It is more active for dogs and other furry animals that face the camera, are large in the frame, and fill most of it with little visible horizon or straight lines (rows 4, 6, 7, 8 and 17 are high for the similar units as well). Nothing checked on new photos turned out to be particular to this unit. The apparent preference for left-facing over right-facing subjects (rows 1 and 3) and for subjects cut off by the photo border (row 10) fell to about the 50th percentile on new photos. So the left-right asymmetry was likely noise. The remaining distinctive-looking rows, such as row 13, rest on very few photos (9 and 6) and sit at the threshold, so none is reliable enough to count as describing this unit specifically.
